werk/the-jimi-hendrix-experience-electri.text:
Electric Ladyland is the third and final studio album by The Jimi Hendrix Experience and was released in October 1968 as a double album. It is the only album by the group on which Jimi Hendrix alone is credited as producer. Recording began in July 1967, took place at several locations and continued in April 1968 at the new Record Plant in New York. Hendrix demanded many takes, and guests streamed into the studio. Producer Chas Chandler quit the project out of frustration.

The result is broad and studio-driven: psychedelic pop, a long blues jam in Voodoo Chile, rhythm and blues, and his version of Bob Dylan's All Along the Watchtower, which even Dylan himself praised. Engineer Eddie Kramer experimented with reversed tape, echo and flanging. Critics did not quite know what to make of it at the time, but the album spent two weeks at number 1 in America and is now regarded as one of his finest works.
werk/the-jimi-hendrix-experience-electri.listen: Listen to Voodoo Chile and notice the long jam with Steve Winwood on organ and Jack Casady on bass. Can you hear how it is blues, but with all the room in the world to stretch out?

werk/the-killers-mr-brightside.text: In June 2004 Hot Fuss was released, the debut album by The Killers from Las Vegas. They sounded British, with synthesizers and the energy of 1980s new wave. Mr. Brightside, about jealousy, became one of the best-known rock songs of the century. In England it stayed in the charts for years. Rock bands could still score worldwide hits, but there would be fewer and fewer of them.
werk/the-killers-mr-brightside.listen: Mr. Brightside has only one verse: after the chorus the song starts again with exactly the same words. Listen to how it still keeps getting more exciting.

werk/the-killers-sam-s-town.text:
Sam's Town is the second studio album by The Killers, released on 27 September 2006 by Island Records. The title comes from Sam's Town Hotel and Gambling Hall in Las Vegas, the band's home town. Singer Brandon Flowers wanted to make a record that showed what had shaped him. Influences cited include U2, Bruce Springsteen and Tom Petty. On the debut he had used Auto-Tune; this time he deliberately did not, so that his voice could be heard for real for the first time.

Critics were divided. The Observer gave it five stars and heard similarities with Springsteen's Born to Run, while Rolling Stone rejected the attempt to sound weighty in the manner of Springsteen. Over the years appreciation grew. Readers of Rolling Stone named it the most underrated album of the decade in 2009, and Q counted it among the best albums of the century. When You Were Young became the big single.
werk/the-killers-sam-s-town.listen: Listen to When You Were Young and notice how unpolished and direct the vocals sound.

werk/the-kingston-trio-here-we-go-again.text:
In 1959 the Kingston Trio were at the height of the folk revival. For this album the three singers received help from Lou Gottlieb in choosing the songs and arrangements. They rehearsed at the Cocoanut Grove, the club where they were performing at the time. Producer Voyle Gilmore recorded it in Studio B in Los Angeles and for the first time used a technique called double-voicing: the three voices were recorded twice and layered over each other, so that the whole sounded fuller.

The repertoire consists mainly of old folk songs and new songs in that style. Molly Dee was written by John Stewart, who would later replace Dave Guard in the trio. Across the Wide Missouri is their version of Oh Shenandoah, and A Worried Man goes back to a song by the Carter Family. The album spent eight weeks at number one and earned Grammy nominations. That year the group had four albums in the top ten at the same time.
werk/the-kingston-trio-here-we-go-again.listen: In A Worried Man, listen to how the three voices together form one full sound. Notice the echo around the instruments.

werk/the-kingston-trio-sold-out.text:
Sold Out was released in 1960 and is the third album by the American folk trio to reach number 1. It stayed there for twelve weeks and was certified gold the same year. El Matador was the first single and only just made the top forty. The album itself spent 54 weeks in that top forty, longer than any other album by the trio. The cover features the model Dolores Erickson.

The band consisted of Dave Guard, Bob Shane, Nick Reynolds and bassist David Buck Wheat, with banjo, guitars and bongos. Raspberries, Strawberries is a new version of the follow-up to the earlier hit Tom Dooley. Two songs from these sessions were released only later, on an anthology. Matt Fink of AllMusic called the album solid and pleasant to listen to, though not challenging. In 1992 and 2001 it was reissued together with String Along.
werk/the-kingston-trio-sold-out.listen: Listen to With Her Head Tucked Underneath Her Arm and notice how the vocals and the accompaniment tell the story together.

werk/the-kingston-trio-string-along.text:
String Along was released in 1960 and was the fifth consecutive studio album by the American folk trio to reach number 1 on the Billboard chart. It stayed there for ten weeks. It was also the last album by the group to reach that position. In 1962 it was certified gold, a year after Dave Guard had left the group. On this album he played the first twelve-string guitar made by Gibson.

The singles were Bad Man's Blunder and Everglades. The Escape of Old John Webb is an old English folk song that was recorded on purpose to make the trio better known in Great Britain. Producer Voyle Gilmore left the closing words Bang, you're dead of Bad Man's Blunder off the single. Bruce Eder of AllMusic considered the album the most unusual of the series and a quieter record, with Ray Charles's Leave My Woman Alone as one of its highlights.
werk/the-kingston-trio-string-along.listen: Listen to Leave My Woman Alone, a song by Ray Charles, and notice what the trio does with a song from another corner of music.

werk/the-kinks-arthur-or-the-decline-and.text:
In early 1969 the British television company Granada asked Ray Davies to make something for television. Together with writer Julian Mitchell he devised a play, with a soundtrack by the Kinks. The play never materialised, but the record did. The story is about Arthur Morgan, a carpet layer, who is based on the brother-in-law of the Davies brothers.

The band made the album at a difficult time. Their previous record, The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society, had failed commercially and bassist Pete Quaife had left. John Dalton took his place. Recording ran from 1 May 1969 and was largely finished by the end of that month. Arranger Lew Warburton wrote the strings. The album was released on 10 October 1969. It sold poorly but received almost unanimous praise, especially from the American music press. Victoria brought the band back into the American charts after two years.
werk/the-kinks-arthur-or-the-decline-and.listen: Listen to Victoria and notice how the guitars and the rhythm immediately give a song about old England a great deal of energy.

werk/the-kinks-face-to-face.text:
Face to Face was released on 28 October 1966 and was the fourth studio album by the Kinks. It was their first album consisting entirely of their own songs. Ray Davies had suffered a nervous breakdown just before the main recording sessions, and the year was full of problems: bassist Pete Quaife was injured, there were legal disputes and a hectic touring schedule. The album left behind the rough beat music of 1964 and leaned on baroque pop and music hall.

Davies increasingly wrote as an observer, with satire on English culture, class differences and the music industry. He wanted to stitch the songs together with sound effects, but Pye Records forced him to make an ordinary album. Sunny Afternoon had already been number 1 in England shortly before. The reception at the time was lukewarm, but the album later gained appreciation and is regarded as one of the first concept albums in rock.
werk/the-kinks-face-to-face.listen: Listen to Party Line and notice the sound effects that connect the songs. Can you hear how Davies tried to make the album sound like one whole?

werk/the-kinks-kinda-kinks.text:
Kinda Kinks is the second studio album by the Kinks. Pye released it in the United Kingdom on 5 March 1965; the American release on Reprise followed on 11 August and differs: three tracks are missing and the singles Set Me Free and Everybody's Gonna Be Happy have been added. Recording took place right after a tour of Asia, and everything was finished and released within two weeks.

The result was a rushed production. Ray Davies was not satisfied: producer Shel Talmy had left too many rough edges in. Even so, the record contained better songs than the debut. Tired of Waiting for You became a number 1 in the British singles chart and the album reached number 3. AllMusic called it uneven, but saw a growing craftsmanship in Davies's songwriting.
werk/the-kinks-kinda-kinks.listen: In Tired of Waiting for You, listen to the melody and notice how directly the song is built.

werk/the-kinks-something-else-by-the-kin.text:
On this album Ray Davies took over production from Shel Talmy, who until then had overseen the Kinks' recordings. The songs were written between the autumn of 1966 and the summer of 1967, when the band toured less and accumulated songs for Davies's still vague Village Green plan. He himself later doubted whether he should have been allowed to produce the record.

The sound is softer than the raw rock and roll of before: acoustic baroque pop, English music hall and tempered R&B, with highlights such as the bossa nova of No Return and the chamber pop of Death of a Clown, a song by Dave Davies. Ray Davies's lyrics deal with English subjects and character types, as in David Watts, Two Sisters and Waterloo Sunset. The album sold poorly, although the singles reached the British top three. Later it grew into a cult favourite, and critics praise the quiet music that carries his characters so beautifully.
werk/the-kinks-something-else-by-the-kin.listen: In Waterloo Sunset, listen to how calm the music stays and notice how the lyrics sketch a picture.

werk/the-kinks-the-kink-kontroversy.text:
This third studio album by the Kinks was released on 26 November 1965 by Pye Records in England. Shel Talmy was the producer. The title mocks the bad reputation the group had acquired the year before, with fights on stage and riots at concerts in Europe. As a result the band was banned from performing in the United States.

It is a transitional record. Milk Cow Blues is still strongly influenced by the blues, and Till the End of the Day resembles the powerful hits of the preceding years. Songs such as The World Keeps Going Round and I'm on an Island already point ahead to the way Ray Davies would later write. Till the End of the Day became a big hit in England. AllMusic called the album the moment when the Kinks grew up, with more considered work than their raw beginnings.
werk/the-kinks-the-kink-kontroversy.listen: Listen to Where Have All the Good Times Gone and notice the allusions in the lyrics to songs by The Beatles and The Rolling Stones.

werk/the-mamas-en-the-papas-if-you-can-b.text:
The debut album by The Mamas & the Papas was released in February 1966 on Dunhill Records. The producer was Lou Adler. The group consisted of Denny Doherty, Cass Elliot and the married couple John and Michelle Phillips, supported by session musicians. The album cover caused an uproar: the four sat in a bathtub with a toilet in the background, which was considered indecent. The cover was withdrawn from the shops and replaced.

Musically the album combines folk rock, pop and soul. It centres on the harmony singing, in which the voices play against each other and complement one another. The record includes Monday, Monday and California Dreamin'. Contemporary critics praised how well the voices were attuned to each other. Later reviewers saw it as their most important work. It is the only album by the group to top the Billboard 200.
werk/the-mamas-en-the-papas-if-you-can-b.listen: In California Dreamin', listen to how the voices take turns taking over the melody and the accompaniment, and notice the flute solo.

werk/the-manhattan-transfer-coming-out.text:
Coming Out is the third album by The Manhattan Transfer and was released on 19 August 1976 on Atlantic Records. The group consisted of Tim Hauser, Laurel Massé, Alan Paul and Janis Siegel. It is a varied collection of covers, ranging from Jesse Stone and Holland-Dozier-Holland to Todd Rundgren and Michael Franks.

Chanson d'Amour became a hit and spent three weeks at number one in the United Kingdom. On Zindy Lou, Ringo Starr and Jim Keltner play drums, Dr. John plays piano and Doug Thorngren plays percussion. On Poinciana (The Song of the Tree) you can hear a solo by Michael Brecker. In 1993 the record was reissued on CD.
werk/the-manhattan-transfer-coming-out.listen: Listen to Poinciana (The Song of the Tree) and notice Michael Brecker's solo between the vocals.

werk/the-manhattan-transfer-extensions.text:
Extensions was released on 31 October 1979 on Atlantic Records and was the fifth studio album by The Manhattan Transfer. It marked a new phase. Cheryl Bentyne had replaced Laurel Massé in early 1979, and Jay Graydon sat behind the controls as producer for the first time. It was also the first album with songs that were successful in both jazz and pop.

Twilight Zone/Twilight Tone reached number thirty on the Hot 100. The best-known track is Birdland, a composition by Weather Report for which Jon Hendricks wrote a vocalese lyric. It won a Grammy, and Janis Siegel received one for her vocal arrangement. The New York Times saw the group as the heirs of Lambert, Hendricks and Ross.
werk/the-manhattan-transfer-extensions.listen: In Birdland, listen to how the voices take over the instrumental parts of the original. Notice the fast lyrics that Hendricks wrote over them.

werk/the-moody-blues-days-of-future-pass.text:
Days of Future Passed is the second album by the Moody Blues and was released on 17 November 1967 on Deram Records. The group had started out as a rhythm and blues band, but ran into money troubles at the end of 1966 and went through personnel changes. Justin Hayward and John Lodge joined, Tony Clarke became producer and Mike Pinder played the Mellotron. Together they struck out in a new direction with their own songs instead of covers.

Deram wanted to present pop and classical music with an orchestra in order to show off stereo technology. The band instead made their own songs about one day in the life of an ordinary person, interrupted by orchestral music arranged and conducted by Peter Knight. Nights in White Satin, written by Hayward, became the big hit. The album did reasonably well on release, but through radio play grew into an American top 10 hit. It is regarded as one of the first progressive rock albums and concept albums.
werk/the-moody-blues-days-of-future-pass.listen: Listen to Nights in White Satin and notice the Mellotron and the orchestra. Can you hear how together they make a string-like sound?

werk/the-moody-blues-in-search-of-the-lo.text:
In Search of the Lost Chord is the third album by The Moody Blues and was released in July 1968 on Deram. The success of Days of Future Passed gave the group more studio time and freedom. Producer Tony Clarke recorded the album between May and June in Decca's Studio One in West Hampstead, largely on four tracks. Only Legend of a Mind dates from as early as January 1968.

Like its predecessor it is a concept album, this time centred on quest and discovery, of the world as well as of one's own inner self. The music is influenced by psychedelia and by meditation and Eastern spirituality. The album opens with a poem by Graeme Edge and closes with Om, an ode to the mantra. Ride My See-Saw was the first single. Ray Thomas wrote Dr. Livingstone, I Presume as a cheerful counterpart to the more serious songs. Justin Hayward later said that the band found its soul and direction here.
werk/the-moody-blues-in-search-of-the-lo.listen: Listen to Ride My See-Saw and notice the driving rhythm and the three- and four-part harmony singing in the middle section.

werk/the-moody-blues-on-the-threshold-of.text:
On the Threshold of a Dream is the fourth album by the Moody Blues and was released in April 1969 on Deram. It was recorded in January 1969, straight after the first tour of North America, nine months after In Search of the Lost Chord. It was the group's first number 1 in the United Kingdom. It is a concept album with a looser theme than the earlier records. The title, devised by Mike Pinder, refers to the flower-power hope that society stood on the threshold of a new consciousness.

Each band member contributed ideas to that theme. Together they worked out the songs, says John Lodge. The record opens with a spoken introduction by drummer Graeme Edge, inspired by Descartes's cogito, ergo sum. Justin Hayward called the album the group's defining work.
werk/the-moody-blues-on-the-threshold-of.listen: Listen to In the Beginning: notice the spoken introduction in which a narrator first doubts his own existence and then affirms it.

werk/the-moody-blues-the-magnificent-moo.text:
The Magnificent Moodies is the 1965 debut album by the British band The Moody Blues, released on Decca Records. It is the only record by the first line-up, with Denny Laine, Clint Warwick, Mike Pinder, Ray Thomas and Graeme Edge. The producer was Denny Cordell, except on Go Now, which Alex Wharton produced and which had been a number 1 in the charts earlier that year.

The album mixes rhythm and blues covers with original songs by Laine and Pinder, which lean more towards Merseybeat. It also includes a cover of the Gershwin song It Ain't Necessarily So. The back cover carries a prose poem by Donovan. Among those at the party celebrating the release were George Harrison, Paul McCartney, Marianne Faithfull and Sandie Shaw. The record did not reach the British chart, but reached number 5 in the New Musical Express. Warwick and Laine left in 1966, after which Justin Hayward and John Lodge joined.
werk/the-moody-blues-the-magnificent-moo.listen: Listen to Go Now and notice how the band, as a young group, plays rhythm and blues here.

werk/the-mothers-of-invention-freak-out.text:
The Mothers of Invention were originally a bar band, the Soul Giants, who played rhythm and blues covers. After Frank Zappa joined the group, his own work came to the fore and the name changed. In early 1966 producer Tom Wilson offered them a contract with Verve, under the impression that they were a white blues band. When he heard Who Are the Brain Police? he realised that this was not so, and Zappa was given an almost unlimited budget.

The record was released on 27 June 1966 as a double album and is regarded as one of the first concept albums in rock: a satire on American pop culture and on the emerging freak scene in Los Angeles. The music ranges from rhythm and blues, doo-wop and blues rock to orchestral arrangements and avant-garde sound collages. In the United States the album initially received a lukewarm reception; in Europe it was a success. Later it acquired cult status and, in 1999, a Grammy Hall of Fame Award.
werk/the-mothers-of-invention-freak-out.listen: Listen to Trouble Every Day and notice how a bluesy song is used to comment on a current news event.

werk/the-mothers-of-invention-we-re-only.text:
We're Only in It for the Money is the third album by the Mothers of Invention and was released on 4 March 1968 on Verve Records. Frank Zappa wrote and composed it as a concept album. The main recording sessions ran from July to September 1967 at Mayfair Studios in New York. When the Beatles released Sgt. Pepper, Zappa decided to turn the record into a parody of it, because he found the Beatles insincere and felt they were only in it for the money. Verve, fearing a lawsuit, dared to use the parody cover only as an inner sleeve.

The album pokes fun at the left and the right, at hippie culture and at the commercialisation of youth culture. Zappa used recording techniques and tape editing for short songs, interrupted by dialogue and unrelated music. Verve and MGM censored the record heavily. Surprisingly, the hippies embraced the album. In 2005 it was added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry.
werk/the-mothers-of-invention-we-re-only.listen: Listen to Concentration Moon and notice the way spoken passages and music alternate. Can you hear how the lyrics combine satire and studio tricks?

werk/the-notorious-b-i-g-ready-to-die.text:
The debut of The Notorious B.I.G. was recorded in two phases, in 1993 and 1994, mainly at The Hit Factory in New York. The first tracks, such as Ready to Die and Gimme the Loot, are darker and less suited to radio. When Sean Combs was fired from Uptown, the record was shelved for a while. Combs started Bad Boy Records, and there Biggie finished the album, with a smoother and more confident voice. Now came the songs with a better chance in the charts, such as Juicy and Big Poppa.

The production comes largely from Easy Mo Bee and the Hitmen and relies on samples, with a heavy bottom end and occasionally blues guitar. Biggie tells, in part autobiographically, of his life as a young criminal, and critics especially praised his storytelling. The record breathed new life into East Coast hip hop at a time when the West Coast ruled commercially. It was the only album released during his lifetime.
werk/the-notorious-b-i-g-ready-to-die.listen: Listen to Juicy and notice how he tells his life story, from his childhood to his success.

werk/the-o-jays-back-on-top.text:
Back on Top is the third album by the O'Jays and was released in 1968 on the Bell label. George Kerr produced it, Pat Jaques was the engineer and Richard Tee was conductor and arranger. The four remaining original members sing on it: Eddie Levert, William Powell, Walter Williams and Bobby Massey. They all appear on the cover as well. It is the first record without Bill Isles, who left the group shortly before the recording. Massey would leave later, just before their breakthrough success at Philadelphia International Records.

The most important song is I'll Be Sweeter Tomorrow (Than I Was Today), their biggest hit for Bell. Look Over Your Shoulder also became a hit. Between the tracks sits I'll Be Seeing You, a standard by Irving Kahal and Sammy Fain. The rest was written by, among others, George Kerr, Walter Williams and Richard and Robert Poindexter.
werk/the-o-jays-back-on-top.listen: Listen to I'll Be Sweeter Tomorrow (Than I Was Today) and notice how the four voices sound together. Who takes the lead, and when do the others join in?

werk/the-o-jays-back-stabbers.text:
Back Stabbers is the sixth studio album by the O'Jays, a soul group from Philadelphia consisting of Eddie Levert, Walter Williams and William Powell. It was released in August 1972 on Philadelphia International Records and was recorded that year at Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia.

For the group it was a breakthrough. The album reached the top ten of the Billboard Pop Albums chart and sold more than half a million copies within a year. Two of the group's biggest singles are on it, Back Stabbers and Love Train. Critics regard it as a milestone of early 1970s soul, a few even as the high point of Philly soul. In 2012 it ranked number 318 in Rolling Stone's list of the five hundred greatest albums of all time.
werk/the-o-jays-back-stabbers.listen: Listen to Back Stabbers and notice how the three singers carry the song together.

werk/the-o-jays-ship-ahoy.text:
Ship Ahoy is the seventh album by the O'Jays and was released in 1973 on Philadelphia International Records. It is conceived as a concept album around the title song, which Gamble and Huff had first written for the soundtrack of Shaft in Africa. That song lasts almost ten minutes and is about African prisoners on a slave ship. The sounds of waves and cracking whips make the story immediate. The cover, too, with the group in a slave hold, was striking.

Besides these songs of social comment there are love songs. For the Love of Money, built around a bass line by Anthony Jackson, protests against materialism. Put Your Hands Together sounds hopeful, with a strong gospel feel. The album reached number 1 on the Billboard Black Albums chart and The New York Times praised it as Gamble and Huff at their most creative.
werk/the-o-jays-ship-ahoy.listen: Listen to For the Love of Money and notice the bass line around which the song is built.

werk/the-offspring-americana.text:
Americana is the fifth studio album by The Offspring and was released on 17 November 1998 on Columbia Records. After a world tour for Ixnay on the Hombre, the band started on new work in July 1998. Recording lasted about two months and took place with Dave Jerden, for the second and last time. Singer Dexter Holland did not want to make a radically different record. When a few songs about the America of 1998 were ready, the band saw a theme: a commentary on American culture, inspired by, among other things, the Jerry Springer Show.

The album entered at number two on the Billboard 200, the band's highest position, and produced the hits Pretty Fly (For a White Guy), Why Don't You Get a Job and The Kids Aren't Alright. Pretty Fly has a Latin flavour and Pay the Man is psychedelic, built without repeating sections. It had been left off the previous record because it sounded too different.
werk/the-offspring-americana.listen: Listen to Pay the Man and notice that the song has no repeating verse or chorus.

werk/the-offspring-ignition.text:
Ignition was released in September 1992 and was the second album by The Offspring. In 1991 the group had recorded the EP Baghdad with producer Thom Wilson. Thanks to its success they signed with Epitaph, the label of Brett Gurewitz of Bad Religion. In June 1992 they recorded Ignition at two studios, Westbeach Recorders and Track Record. Part of the material consisted of renewed versions of older songs, such as Get It Right and Take It Like a Man.

This is fast, melodic punk rock in a time of grunge and alternative rock. The record did not enter the Billboard 200, but the group gained a growing audience in Southern California and toured for a year and a half. Only in 1996, after the success of Smash, did the album go gold. Critics have since regarded Ignition as one of the group's best records. Guitar World ranked it number two in its list of guitar albums of 1992.
werk/the-offspring-ignition.listen: Listen to Kick Him When He's Down and notice the tempo and the guitars, in which you can hear the group's punk rock before its commercial success.

werk/the-offspring-ixnay-on-the-hombre.text:
Ixnay on the Hombre, released on 4 February 1997, is the fourth album by The Offspring and their debut on a major label, Columbia Records. After the enormous success of Smash the band went into the studio in June 1996, for the first time not with Thom Wilson but with producer Dave Jerden. The move caused tension with Epitaph founder Brett Gurewitz, and for that reason the record was still released by Epitaph in Europe.

The album entered at number nine on the Billboard 200 and was well received by critics and fans. Four singles were released: All I Want, Gone Away, The Meaning of Life and I Choose. Pay the Man was recorded in these sessions but ended up later on Americana. Change the World elaborates on a hidden track from Smash and itself contains a hidden spoken fragment by Larry Bud Melman.
werk/the-offspring-ixnay-on-the-hombre.listen: Listen to Change the World and find the hidden spoken fragment by Larry Bud Melman that is tucked away in the song.

werk/the-offspring-smash.text:
For their third album The Offspring went to Track Record in North Hollywood in January 1994. They recorded it in twenty days, with producer Thom Wilson. The budget was small: twenty thousand dollars. The band kept looking for an empty studio to slip into cheaply, and the last four songs came about in two nights. The previous album Ignition had not brought the big breakthrough, and nobody expected radio success.

Yet Smash became exactly that. Thanks to the rise of grunge, punk rock gained a wider audience. Come Out and Play reached number one on the Billboard Modern Rock chart, and Self Esteem and Gotta Get Away also became hits. Together with Green Day's Dookie the record brought punk into the mainstream and paved the way for the pop punk of the 1990s. The album mostly received positive reviews and became the best-selling album ever released by an independent label.
werk/the-offspring-smash.listen: Listen to What Happened to You? and notice the ska beat that carries the song. How does it differ from the rest of the album?

werk/the-police-reggatta-de-blanc.text:
Reggatta de Blanc, loosely translated White Reggae, is the second album by The Police. The group recorded it in four weeks, spread over several months, again at Surrey Sound with Nigel Gray. A&M wanted a bigger studio and a better-known producer, but the band chose otherwise. There was little new material, so Sting and Stewart Copeland dug out old songs and ideas. The lyrics of Bring On the Night, for example, were already three years old.

The music blends hard rock, British pop, reggae and new wave. The title song is an instrumental that grew out of the live shows and earned the band a Grammy. Message in a Bottle and Walking on the Moon became the group's first British number 1 singles, and the album itself topped the charts in Great Britain, Australia and the Netherlands. A Rolling Stone reviewer wrote that the energy of the rhythmic counterattacks made any objections to the borrowed styles beside the point.
werk/the-police-reggatta-de-blanc.listen: In Reggatta de Blanc, the instrumental title track, listen to Stewart Copeland's drumming and to how the band builds tension without vocals.

werk/the-prodigy-always-outnumbered-neve.text:
After the tour for The Fat of the Land the group started on a new album, but the work dragged on for years: recording ran from September 1998 to April 2004. Liam Howlett at first did not like the new sound, took a break in 2000 and got going again in 2001 with producer Neil McLellan, after four months had produced nothing. He made the record almost entirely alone, with the program Propellerhead Reason on a laptop. Keith Flint and Maxim Reality do not take part, the only time in the group's history.

There is more singing than on the previous record, from guests such as Juliette Lewis, Liam and Noel Gallagher, Kool Keith and Twista. Spitfire opens as a tribute to the Second World War aircraft. The album entered at number one in England, but the reviews were mixed.
werk/the-prodigy-always-outnumbered-neve.listen: Listen to Medusa's Path, an instrumental of six minutes, and notice the moment when Phoenix's synthesizer comes in.

werk/the-prodigy-invaders-must-die.text:
Invaders Must Die was released on 23 February 2009 on the new label Take Me to the Hospital. Recording began in February 2006, shortly after the compilation Their Law, and ended in November 2008. Liam Howlett saw the record as a mashup of the previous albums. After Leeroy Thornhill's departure, all band members took part in the writing for the first time. It is also the group's only album without explicit tracks.

The title song was first a free download. James Rushent co-produced it together with Omen, which reached number four in England. Dave Grohl plays drums on Run with the Wolves, and Stand Up is the only instrumental. Critics reacted in a mixed way, but the album topped the charts in England, for the fourth time in a row.
werk/the-prodigy-invaders-must-die.listen: Listen to Run with the Wolves and notice the drums of Dave Grohl, the guest on this track.

werk/the-prodigy-music-for-the-jilted-ge.text:
The second album by The Prodigy was released on 4 July 1994 on XL Recordings. It is partly a reaction to the British rave scene, which became corrupted by its own success, and to the Criminal Justice Act of 1994, which cracked down on raves. In Their Law you can hear this in a spoken intro and the line Fuck 'em and their law. Liam Howlett later called the title stupid himself and said the record had never been meant politically.

The music blends breakbeat, techno and hardcore with heavy bass lines and aggressive beats. Tracks such as No Good (Start the Dance) and Voodoo People helped shape the electronic scene of the 1990s. Many samples come from films, such as Star Wars in Full Throttle. Critical reception was glowing: NME called it a stormy requiem, and the record was nominated for the Mercury Music Prize.
werk/the-prodigy-music-for-the-jilted-ge.listen: In Voodoo People, listen to the guitar riff that sounds between the electronic beats, and notice how hard and tight the rhythm stays.

werk/the-prodigy-the-fat-of-the-land.text:
On The Prodigy's third record Liam Howlett wrote almost all the music himself, while Maxim Reality can be heard on two tracks. Recording dragged on for months, because after Firestarter Howlett preferred to play PlayStation rather than sit in the studio. His record company was on his back. The album was released on 30 June 1997 on XL Recordings. The cover shows a horseshoe crab; the title refers to an English expression for living well and richly.

The record brought rave and rock closer together: the magazine Metal Hammer later saw in it the point where the rave club and metal culture collided. Smack My Bitch Up caused an outcry, because an American women's organisation found the song sexist. The group themselves said the song is about doing everything in an intense way. Reviews were glowing and the album topped the charts in the United Kingdom and the United States. It became their best-selling album.
werk/the-prodigy-the-fat-of-the-land.listen: Listen to Firestarter and notice how electronic beats and the raw energy of rock come together here. Can you hear why this song fitted both dance and metal?

werk/the-rolling-stones-aftermath.text:
The Rolling Stones recorded Aftermath in December 1965 and March 1966 at RCA Studios in California, in the breaks between their tours. It was the first album to consist entirely of original songs by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards. The title came about more or less by chance: the original title Could You Walk on the Water? was dropped by the American label for fear of offending Christians. The British release ran to well over 52 minutes, the longest for a pop record up to that time.

Brian Jones returned as an important contributor and played instruments that were unusual in pop music, such as the sitar, Appalachian dulcimer, Japanese koto and marimba. Besides blues and rhythm and blues, influences of folk, country, psychedelia, baroque and Middle Eastern music can be heard. The lyrics are dark and sarcastic, with women as prominent characters, which offended some listeners. The record spent eight weeks at the top of the British chart and is regarded as the group's first classic album.
werk/the-rolling-stones-aftermath.listen: Listen to Under My Thumb and notice the marimba, an instrument you rarely hear in rock, which carries the rhythm of the song.

werk/the-rolling-stones-beggars-banquet.text:
Beggars Banquet was released on 6 December 1968 and was the seventh album by the Rolling Stones, the first under producer Jimmy Miller. After the psychedelic pop records Between the Buttons and Their Satanic Majesties Request, the group returned to roots and blues. Brian Jones was unreliable in the studio because of his drug use, so Keith Richards recorded almost all the guitar parts. Even so, Jones played on eight tracks, including sitar and tanpura on Street Fighting Man.

The album is instrumentally adventurous, with Latin rhythms, claves, tabla, shehnai and congas. A fine example is Sympathy for the Devil, with hypnotic African rhythms. Street Fighting Man became an eternal radio favourite. The record company rejected the first cover, showing a scrawled-on toilet wall, which delayed the release by months. Critics saw the album as a return to former strength, and it has been inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
werk/the-rolling-stones-beggars-banquet.listen: Listen to Sympathy for the Devil and notice the hypnotic rhythms beneath Jagger's vocals. Can you hear how the congas keep driving the song onwards?

werk/the-rolling-stones-between-the-butt.text:
Between the Buttons was released on 20 January 1967 and was the fifth studio album by the Rolling Stones. Recording ran from August 1966 in Los Angeles and London, including at Olympic Sound Studios. It was the last album that Andrew Loog Oldham produced entirely. Brian Jones often left his guitar lying and played vibraphone, electric dulcimer, banjo, kazoo, theremin and saxophone.

The result is an eclectic album with influences of psychedelia, baroque pop and music hall, with piano by, among others, Ian Stewart, Jack Nitzsche and Nicky Hopkins. Mick Jagger himself was not happy with it: according to him the sound was lost through the repeated bouncing down of the four-track tapes. Critics were more positive later. Robert Christgau called it underrated, and the American version with Ruby Tuesday appears in Rolling Stone's list of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/the-rolling-stones-between-the-butt.listen: Listen to Ruby Tuesday and notice the piano and the way the song stays gentle and melodic. Can you hear how far this sounds from the raw blues rock you would expect from the band?

werk/the-rolling-stones-december-s-child.text:
December's Children (and Everybody's) was, in November 1965, the Rolling Stones' fifth American album, but not really a true album. There were no separate recording sessions. The record consists mainly of songs from earlier British albums, singles and EPs that had not yet been heard in America, supplemented with a few unused recordings. Most of the tracks were recorded on 5 and 6 September 1965 at the RCA studio in Hollywood. Jagger later called it a collection of songs. The title came from manager Andrew Loog Oldham.

It is the last early album with many covers: Jagger and Richards wrote only half of it themselves. The record includes Get Off of My Cloud, the group's second American number 1. It also features As Tears Go By, their own version of a song that Marianne Faithfull had recorded earlier. The album reached number 4 in the United States and went gold.
werk/the-rolling-stones-december-s-child.listen: Listen to As Tears Go By and notice what is missing: no electric guitar, bass or drums, but acoustic guitar and strings.

werk/the-rolling-stones-exile-on-main-st.text:
In 1971 the Rolling Stones discovered that, through financial mismanagement by their manager Allen Klein, they had paid far too little tax, and they had to leave England. Keith Richards rented the villa Nellcôte in the south of France. In the basement an improvised studio was built using the band's mobile recording truck. The sessions lasted deep into the night and the line-up changed from day to day. Overdubs followed at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles, with, among others, Nicky Hopkins, Bobby Keys and producer Jimmy Miller.

It became the group's first double album, with influences from blues, rock 'n' roll, swing, country and gospel. Happy, with Richards as singer, came about during an afternoon jam with baritone sax, guitar and drums. Tumbling Dice became a worldwide top hit. The first reactions were mixed, but at the end of the 1970s a strong reappraisal followed. It is now regarded as a turning point in rock.
werk/the-rolling-stones-exile-on-main-st.listen: In Happy, listen to the singing of Keith Richards: the guitarist sings the lead part himself here.

werk/the-rolling-stones-hackney-diamonds.text:
After the death of drummer Charlie Watts in 2021 the Rolling Stones became more serious about a new album. Their last record of original songs was A Bigger Bang from 2005; after that came only the blues album Blue & Lonesome. Earlier sessions had stalled. On the advice of Paul McCartney, guitarist Ronnie Wood brought in the producer Andrew Watt, who took over the recording in Los Angeles at the end of 2022. They worked like this for about four weeks, followed by two weeks of overdubs.

McCartney plays bass on two tracks. Elton John, Lady Gaga and Stevie Wonder also take part, and former bassist Bill Wyman returned. The album also includes recordings from 2019, with Watts's last studio work. The title is London slang for the broken glass after a burglary. Critics were positive and, for some, considered this the strongest album in decades. It won the Grammy for Best Rock Album.
werk/the-rolling-stones-hackney-diamonds.listen: In Angry, the first single, listen to the guitars and to Mick Jagger's vocals. Ask yourself whether this sounds like a band from the past or from the present.

werk/the-rolling-stones-let-it-bleed.text:
Recording began in February 1969 and continued intermittently until November, at Olympic Studios in London and partly in Los Angeles. The band was in turmoil. Brian Jones, the founder, was often absent from the studio or too intoxicated, was dismissed during the sessions and died a month later. He played on only two tracks. Mick Taylor took his place, but Keith Richards played most of the guitar work. Jimmy Miller produced. The album followed Beggars Banquet and, like that album, returned to blues influences, supplemented with gospel and country.

On Gimme Shelter, Merry Clayton sings along. On You Can't Always Get What You Want the London Bach Choir sings, and Miller himself took over the drums because Charlie Watts could not find the rhythm he was after. On You Got the Silver Richards sang a solo lead vocal for the first time. The album reached number one in the United Kingdom.
werk/the-rolling-stones-let-it-bleed.listen: Listen to the beginning of Gimme Shelter and notice the voice of Merry Clayton, which rises above the band in the choruses.

werk/the-rolling-stones-miss-you.text: In May 1978 the Rolling Stones released Miss You, with a disco bass and a tight beat. The Stones went along with the music that was playing in the clubs, and the song became a number one in America. For some of the rock fans it felt like betrayal. A year later, discs were blown up in Chicago at Disco Demolition Night. Did rock have to adapt to what was popular?
werk/the-rolling-stones-miss-you.listen: Hear the bass hopping along in octave jumps, the harmonica and Mick Jagger singing in falsetto.

werk/the-rolling-stones-out-of-our-heads.text:
Out of Our Heads was released in 1965 in two versions with a different cover and different tracks: first in July in the United States, in September in Great Britain. Manager Andrew Loog Oldham produced it. As on the two previous albums, most of it consists of covers of American blues, soul and rhythm and blues, including songs by Marvin Gaye, Solomon Burke and Sam Cooke. In addition there are original songs, six on the American version.

That version also contains The Last Time, Play With Fire and (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction, rock songs that brought the band's roots into a more modern, guitar-driven sound. Satisfaction became their first number one in the United States, and the album also became their first number one on the American album chart. In Great Britain it reached second place. It was the group's last British album to lean on R&B covers: the next one, Aftermath, consisted entirely of original work by Jagger and Richards.
werk/the-rolling-stones-out-of-our-heads.listen: Listen to Play With Fire: notice the harpsichord and the acoustic guitar that you hear alongside the vocals. This makes it sound different from the rock guitars of the other original songs.

werk/the-rolling-stones-some-girls.text:
Around 1976 the popularity of the Rolling Stones was declining: disco and new rock bands dominated, and punk made everything from the sixties seem outdated. Keith Richards also had legal problems after his arrest in Toronto. In Paris the Stones recorded this album at the Pathé Marconi Studios between October 1977 and February 1978. It was the first with Ronnie Wood as a permanent band member, whose slide guitar fitted well with Richards's playing.

Mick Jagger was the main creative force. He drew inspiration from punk and disco, and from New York. He wrote Miss You entirely on his own, with blues harmonica by Sugar Blue. That song became number one in the United States. Beast of Burden also became a hit. Critics saw the record as a return to form, the best since Exile on Main St.
werk/the-rolling-stones-some-girls.listen: In Miss You, listen to Sugar Blue's harmonica. How does this instrument fit into a song with a danceable influence?

werk/the-rolling-stones-sticky-fingers.text:
This was the first album on the new in-house label Rolling Stones Records, in April 1971, after the end of the contract with Decca and London. It was also the first studio album without the late Brian Jones, and Mick Taylor now played on a whole studio record for the first time. Producer Jimmy Miller kept it simple: drums, guitar, bass and percussion, without the unusual instruments of earlier albums. Brown Sugar, Wild Horses and You Gotta Move were recorded in December 1969 at Muscle Shoals in Alabama, the rest largely in the mobile studio at Stargroves in 1970.

Andy Warhol devised the cover, with a real zip in a pair of jeans. According to Rolling Stone it is the group's bleakest, most drug-tinged album, on which Taylor brings jazz and country into his playing. It became the first album to reach number 1 in both England and America. Brown Sugar topped the Billboard Hot 100.
werk/the-rolling-stones-sticky-fingers.listen: Listen to Brown Sugar and notice the simple set-up of guitar, bass, drums and percussion: the sound has deliberately been pared back to the basics.

werk/the-roots-do-you-want-more.text:
Do You Want More?!!!??! is the second studio album by the Roots and their debut on a major label. It was released on 17 January 1995 on DGC Records, two years after the independent debut Organix from 1993. On some editions the numbering continues on from Organix, which had seventeen tracks, so that the opening track appears as track 18.

Critics regard the record as a classic of jazz rap. The Source included it in a list of the hundred best rap albums in 1998. In 2015, twenty years after its release, the album was certified gold by the RIAA for 500,000 copies sold in the United States. The master tapes, with some unreleased tracks, were lost in the fire on the Universal Studios lot in 2008.
werk/the-roots-do-you-want-more.listen: Listen to the title song Do You Want More?!!!??! and notice how jazz and rap meet, which critics call a classic of jazz rap.

werk/the-roots-illadelph-halflife.text:
Illadelph Halflife is the third studio album by the American hip hop band the Roots, released on 24 September 1996 on DGC and Geffen. It sounds harder and broader than its predecessor Do You Want More?!!!??! and features programmed drums. The guests come from R&B, such as Amel Larrieux and D'Angelo, and from jazz, such as David Murray, Steve Coleman, Cassandra Wilson and Graham Haynes.

The New York Times called it one of the best rap records of the year, with lyrics that also deal with Bosnia, the Olympic Games and terrorism. Rolling Stone later wrote that the messages gained more focus, with sharp criticism of gangsta rap and lyrics by Black Thought about loyalty and responsibility. The Source included the album in a list of the hundred best rap albums in 1998. The multitracks were lost in a fire in 2008; the original master tape remained intact.
werk/the-roots-illadelph-halflife.listen: Listen to the intro of Section, which was later sampled for the Playground riddim, on which Beenie Man sang Who Am I (Sim Simma) in 1997.

werk/the-roots-phrenology.text:
Phrenology is the fifth studio album by The Roots and was released on 26 November 2002. Recording ran from June 2000 to September 2002 at Electric Lady Studios in New York. It was the follow-up to Things Fall Apart, the 1999 breakthrough record, which had been eagerly awaited. The band largely produced the album themselves, with guests such as Cody ChesnuTT, Musiq Soulchild, Talib Kweli and Jill Scott. The title refers to the discredited pseudoscience that used skull shapes to interpret character, and which in the nineteenth century justified racism.

It is above all a hip hop album, with influences from rock, jazz, techno, hardcore punk and soul. The lyrics deal, among other things, with hip hop culture and its commercialisation. On Something in the Way of Things (In Town), the poet Amiri Baraka recites a poem. Water begins with the age-old Bo Diddley beat and ends as a long instrumental fantasy. The critical response was very positive, and the album featured in many year-end lists for 2002.
werk/the-roots-phrenology.listen: Listen to Water and follow how the song begins with the Bo Diddley beat and ends as a longer instrumental fantasy.

werk/the-roots-the-tipping-point.text:
The Tipping Point was released on 13 July 2004 on Questlove's Okayplayer Records and Geffen Records. It is the sixth album by The Roots and follows Phrenology from 2002. The title refers to the book by the journalist Malcolm Gladwell. The cover shows an edited 1944 police photograph of Malcolm X. The music sounds more varied and more pop-oriented than earlier work, with influences of soul, jazz and funk. The lyrics deal with the art of rapping, political insight and social themes.

Some tracks use samples, such as Star by Sly and the Family Stone and Stay Cool by Al Hirt. I Don't Care ended up in the game Gran Turismo 4. In its first week the album stood at number four on the American chart. Critics were mixed about the production and the lyrics, but most reviews were positive.
werk/the-roots-the-tipping-point.listen: Listen to Star / Pointro and try to pick out the sample of Everybody Is a Star by Sly and the Family Stone.

werk/the-roots-things-fall-apart.text:
Things Fall Apart was released on 23 February 1999 on MCA Records and is regarded as The Roots' breakthrough. Recording took place between 1997 and 1998 at Electric Lady, alongside the work of the Soulquarians, a collective centred on, among others, D'Angelo, Erykah Badu and Common. According to drummer Questlove they recorded some 145 songs and fourteen remained. The title comes from the novel by Chinua Achebe, who in turn took the phrase from Yeats.

The record opens with a clip from the film Mo' Better Blues. On Act Too (The Love of My Life), Common raps about the development of hip hop. Double Trouble with Mos Def was the last track to be added. You Got Me won a Grammy in 2000. It was the group's first album to sell more than 500,000 copies and was called a cornerstone of alternative rap by AllMusic.
werk/the-roots-things-fall-apart.listen: Listen to Act Too (The Love of My Life) and hear how Common raps about the development of hip hop.

werk/the-scene-iedereen-is-van-de-wereld.text: In 1990 Iedereen is van de wereld was released by The Scene, the band of singer Thé Lau. The chorus has the simplicity of a national anthem. It got no further than the Tipparade, but grew into a regular singalong at festivals and has featured in the Top 2000 every year since 1999. Thé Lau died in 2015. A song can also become important slowly.
werk/the-scene-iedereen-is-van-de-wereld.listen: Hear the solid guitar rock and the chorus that sounds like a national anthem.

werk/the-selecter-celebrate-the-bullet.text:
The debut Too Much Pressure had been a success, but after that things went wrong. The band came into conflict with 2 Tone Records and argued over direction. Most wanted new wave in the sound, others did not. In August 1980 recording began at Horizon Studios in Coventry. Bassist Charley Anderson and keyboard player Desmond Brown left the group, and Norman Watt-Roy of Ian Dury and the Blockheads stepped in on bass. The producer was once again Roger Lomas.

Celebrate the Bullet is sombre and tense, with political lyrics about social and racial relations and fear of the Cold War. Bristol and Miami is about the 1980 riots in those two cities. The title single was refused by BBC Radio 1, because a DJ thought it was about the murder of John Lennon. The album reached only number 41 in the British chart.
werk/the-selecter-celebrate-the-bullet.listen: Listen to Bristol and Miami and notice the punky ska rhythms and the energy with which the riots of 1980 are sung about.

werk/the-selecter-pucker.text:
Pucker! followed The Happy Album in 1995. In Great Britain it was released on Dojo, in the United States under the title Hairspray on Triple X. Bassist Nick Welsh now produced alone. Guitarist Paul Seacroft played on it as an unofficial fifth member, and Pauline Black and Arthur Gaps Hendrickson once again shared the vocals of The Selecter.

The sound is a moderate version of ska, with elements of new wave and power pop. For the first time the lyrics are sunny and light, with the exception of the gloomy Then She Did. There are two covers: Sugar Town, with B.J. Cole on pedal steel, and Bob Dylan's Rainy Day Women. The album did not make the charts, but the reviews were mostly positive. Trouser Press called the mix innocently weird and surprisingly pleasant.
werk/the-selecter-pucker.listen: Listen to Sugar Town and try to pick out the pedal steel of guest musician B.J. Cole, an unusual sound for a ska band.

werk/the-selecter-the-happy-album.text:
After the commercial failure of Celebrate the Bullet, the band broke up in 1981. In 1991 The Selecter got back together, which led to the live album Out on the Streets. Founder Neol Davies left after that and Arthur Gaps Hendrickson returned. He and Pauline Black share the vocals. In 1993 recording began at a studio on the Holloway Road in London, with Aswad guitarist Jimmy Senya Haynes as producer. In 1994 the album was released on Demon Music.

The core remains ska, but hip hop, samples, electronics and orchestral sounds are added, plus slow reggae tracks, including the covers I Want Justice and Sweet and Dandy. Despite the title, the lyrics are about social injustice. Critics were glowing. Trouser Press wrote that the album is anything but happy and that this speaks in its favour. It did not enter the British chart.
werk/the-selecter-the-happy-album.listen: Listen to the opener Reselecterization and notice the short instrumental passage that comes from hip hop, before the song drops into a ska rhythm.

werk/the-selecter-too-much-pressure.text:
After the hit single On My Radio, The Selecter, from Coventry, recorded their debut album from December 1979 to January 1980 over two months at Horizon Studios, with producer Errol Ross. Rico Rodriguez and Dick Cuthell of The Specials played the horns. The album is largely a studio version of what the live audience of the time heard: mostly original songs by Neol Davies, supplemented with covers of old ska and reggae.

The music is tense and sharp, a mixture of punk, ska and reggae with raw vocals and politically aware lyrics. Singer Pauline Black stands out for her voice. The record was released on 15 February 1980 on 2 Tone Records and reached number 5 in the British album chart. Later it went gold. The first single, Three Minute Hero, did moderately; Missing Words reached number 23. In the United States, On My Radio was added as the first track.
werk/the-selecter-too-much-pressure.listen: Listen to Three Minute Hero and notice the bouncing ska rhythms and the vocals of Pauline Black.

werk/the-slits-cut.text:
Cut is the debut album by The Slits, an English group with singer Ari Up, guitarist Viv Albertine and bassist Tessa Pollitt. It was recorded at Ridge Farm Studios in Rusper and produced by Dennis Bovell. The album was released on 7 September 1979 on Island Records. The music blends punk and reggae with idiosyncratic art pop, and the group embraced the Jamaican influences completely, as one of the first bands to do so.

The record reached number thirty in the British album chart. Critics called it fun and catchy, despite the rough, unpolished sound. Ari Up's wild singing in particular was praised and later taken up by other post-punk bands. Rolling Stone wrote that bands such as Bikini Kill and Sleater-Kinney came into being because of the album, and Kurt Cobain listed it in his diary among his fifty favourite records. Typical Girls has a separate entry in Rolling Stone's list of the best songs.
werk/the-slits-cut.listen: In Typical Girls, listen to how the vocals, the playful rhythm and the reggae influence together form an idiosyncratic, defiant sound.

werk/the-smashing-pumpkins-adore.text:
Adore followed Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness and the long world tour afterwards. Recording was difficult. Drummer Jimmy Chamberlin had left, Billy Corgan was going through a divorce and his mother died. He later called the record the work of a band falling apart. Recording began in 1997, first in Chicago with producer Brad Wood and then in Los Angeles, where Corgan mostly took charge himself. Without a permanent drummer the band used a drum machine.

The album sounds much calmer than earlier work. Synthesizers, programming, acoustic guitar and piano take the place of heavy guitars. At least five songs revolve mainly around piano, and For Martha is a tribute to Corgan's mother, largely recorded in a live take. Fans were divided and it sold less than its predecessors. Critics, however, were positive about the darker course, and Adore grew into a cult album.
werk/the-smashing-pumpkins-adore.listen: Listen to For Martha and notice how personal and restrained the song sounds, compared with the heavy guitar sound of earlier records.
